paragraphs: So he spoke, and Deiphobus could not decide what to do. He wondered whether to go back and bring some other Trojan to help him, or to take up the challenge alone. In the end he thought it best to fetch Aeneas. He found him standing at the rear of the army, still sore at Priam, who gave him no share of honor to match his brave deeds. Deiphobus went up to him and said, “Aeneas, prince among the Trojans, if you feel any tie of kinship, help me now to defend the husband of your sister. Come with me to save Alcathous. He married your sister and raised you in his house when you were a child, and now Idomeneus has killed him.”

With these words he moved the heart of Aeneas, who went after Idomeneus, eager for great deeds of valor. But Idomeneus was not to be frightened like a small child. He stood his ground like a wild boar at bay in the mountains, waiting for a great crowd of men to reach him in some lonely place. The bristles stand up along its back, its eyes flash fire, and it whets its tusks, eager to defend itself against hounds and men. In just that way famed Idomeneus held firm and did not give way as Aeneas came on. He called out to his comrades, looking toward Ascalaphus, Aphareus, Deipyrus, Meriones and Antilochus, all brave soldiers. “Come to me, my friends,” he cried, “and do not leave me alone. I am in great fear of swift Aeneas, who is coming at me and is a fearsome dealer of death in battle. He is also in the flower of youth, when a man’s strength is greatest. If I were his age and had my present spirit, either he or I would soon carry off the prize of victory.”

At this they all gathered around him as one man, with shields on their shoulders. On the other side Aeneas called to his comrades, looking toward Deiphobus, Paris and Agenor, who led the Trojans together with himself. The people followed them as sheep follow the ram when they go down to drink after feeding, and the shepherd’s heart is glad. In the same way the heart of Aeneas was gladdened when he saw his people follow him.

Then they fought furiously hand to hand over the body of Alcathous, swinging their long spears. The bronze armor on their bodies rang fearfully as they aimed at one another in the crush of the fight. The two heroes Aeneas and Idomeneus, peers of Ares, outdid everyone in their longing to hack at each other with sword and spear. Aeneas took the first throw, but Idomeneus was watching and dodged the spear. It left the strong hand of Aeneas in vain and stuck quivering in the ground. Idomeneus in turn struck Oenomaus in the middle of the belly and broke the plate of his corslet. His bowels came gushing out, and he fell sprawling in the dust, clutching the earth in the palms of his hands. Idomeneus pulled his spear out of the body but could not strip off the rest of Oenomaus’s armor, because a rain of darts was showered on him. His strength was also beginning to fail, so that he could no longer charge. He could not spring forward to recover his own weapon, and he could not swerve aside from one aimed at him. So although he still defended himself in hand-to-hand fighting, his heavy feet could not carry him swiftly out of the battle. Deiphobus threw a spear at him as he slowly retreated from the field, for his bitterness against him was as fierce as ever. Again he missed, and he hit Ascalaphus, the son of Ares. The spear went through his shoulder, and he fell sprawling in the dust, clutching the earth in the palms of his hands.

Grim Ares of the awful voice did not yet know that his son had fallen. He was sitting on the summits of Olympus under the golden clouds, by command of Zeus, where the other gods also sat, forbidden to take part in the battle. Meanwhile the men fought furiously over the body. Deiphobus tore the helmet from the head of Ascalaphus, but Meriones leapt at him and struck him on the arm with a spear. The visored helmet fell from Deiphobus’s hand and came ringing down on the ground. Meriones then sprang on him like a vulture, drew the spear out of his shoulder, and fell back under cover of his men. Then Polites, own brother of Deiphobus, put his arms around Deiphobus’s waist and carried him out of the battle, until he reached his horses. They were standing at the rear of the fight with the chariot and their driver. These took him toward the city, groaning in great pain, with blood flowing from his arm.

The others kept on fighting, and the battle cry rose to heaven without ceasing. Aeneas sprang on Aphareus son of Caletor and struck him with a spear in the throat, which was turned toward him. Aphareus’s head fell to one side, his helmet and shield came down with him, and death, the enemy of life, was poured around him. Antilochus saw his chance and flew at Thoon, wounding him as he turned around. He laid open the vein that runs all the way up the back to the neck, cutting it clean away along its whole length. Thoon fell in the dust on his back, stretching out his hands toward his comrades and pleading for help. Antilochus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders, glaring fearfully around him as he did it. The Trojans closed in on every side and struck his broad, gleaming shield, but they could not wound his body, for Poseidon stood guard over the son of Nestor, though the darts fell thickly around him. He was never clear of the enemy but always in the thick of the fight. His spear was never idle. He poised and aimed it in every direction, so eager was he to hit someone from a distance or to fight him hand to hand.

Adamas, son of Asius, saw him aiming among the crowd. He rushed at him and struck him with a spear in the middle of his shield, but Poseidon made the point useless, for he begrudged Adamas the life of Antilochus. One half of the spear stuck fast in the shield of Antilochus like a charred stake, and the other half lay on the ground. Adamas then drew back under cover of his men, but Meriones went after him and hit him with a spear midway between the private parts and the navel, where a wound is especially painful to wretched mortals. There Meriones transfixed him, and Adamas writhed around the spear like a bull that mountain herdsmen have bound with ropes of withes and are dragging away by force. In the same way he writhed for a while, though not for long, until Meriones came up and drew the spear out of his body, and darkness veiled his eyes.

Then Helenus struck Deipyrus with a great Thracian sword. He hit him on the temple in close combat and tore the helmet from his head. The helmet fell to the ground and rolled at the feet of one of the Achaean fighters, who took charge of it. But the eyes of Deipyrus closed in the darkness of death.

Menelaus was grieved at this and went menacingly at Helenus, brandishing his spear. Helenus drew his bow, and the two attacked at the same moment, one with his spear, the other with his bow and arrow. The son of Priam hit the breastplate of Menelaus’s corslet, but the arrow glanced off it. As black beans or peas come pattering onto a threshing floor from the broad winnowing shovel, blown by shrill winds and shaken by the shovel, so the arrow glanced off and bounced away from the shield of Menelaus. He in his turn wounded the hand that Helenus carried his bow with. The spear went right through the hand and stuck in the bow itself. Helenus retreated under cover of his men to save his life, with his hand dragging at his side, for the spear weighed it down until Agenor pulled it out and bound the hand carefully in a woolen sling that his squire had with him.

Pisander then went straight at Menelaus. His evil destiny was luring him on to his doom, for he was to fall in the fight with you, Menelaus. When the two were close together, the spear of the son of Atreus turned aside and missed. Pisander then struck the shield of brave Menelaus but could not pierce it, for the shield stopped the spear and the shaft broke. Even so he was glad and sure of victory. But the son of Atreus drew his sword at once and sprang at him. Pisander took the bronze battle-axe that hung at his side under his shield, with its long, polished handle of olive wood, and the two went at each other. Pisander struck the peak of Menelaus’s crested helmet just under the crest itself. Menelaus hit Pisander as he came on, on the forehead, just where the nose begins. The bones cracked, and Pisander’s two eyes, drabbled in gore, fell at his feet in the dust. He fell backward to the ground. Menelaus set his heel on him, stripped him of his armor, and boasted over him. “This is how you Trojans will leave the ships of the Achaeans, proud and insatiable for battle as you are. You will not be spared any of the disgrace and shame that you have heaped on me. You cowardly she-wolves, you did not fear the anger of dread Zeus, avenger of violated hospitality, who will one day destroy your city. You stole my wedded wife and wickedly carried off much treasure when you were her guest. Now you want to fling fire on our ships and kill our heroes. A day will come when, rage as you may, you will be stopped. Father Zeus, they say you are above all, both gods and men, in wisdom, and that everything that befalls us comes from you. How can you favor the Trojans like this, men so proud and overbearing that they never tire of fighting? Everything palls after a while: sleep, love, sweet song, stately dance. Still, these are things a man would surely rather have his fill of than of battle, yet it is of battle that the Trojans cannot get enough.”
With that, Menelaus stripped the blood-stained armor from the body of Pisander and handed it to his men. Then he took his place again among those at the front of the fight.

Harpalion, son of King Pylaemenes, then sprang at him. He had come to fight at Troy with his father, and he never went home again. He struck the middle of Menelaus’s shield with his spear but could not pierce it. To save his life he drew back under cover of his men, looking around on every side in case he should be wounded. But Meriones aimed a bronze-tipped arrow at him as he left the field and hit him on the right buttock. The arrow went through the bone and into the bladder. He sat down where he was and breathed his last in the arms of his comrades, stretched like a worm on the ground, watering the earth with the blood that flowed from his wound. The brave Paphlagonians tended him with all due care. They lifted him into his chariot and carried him sadly to the city of Troy. His father went with him, weeping bitterly, but no ransom could bring his dead son back to life.

Paris was deeply grieved by the death of Harpalion, who had been his host when he went among the Paphlagonians, and he aimed an arrow to avenge him. There was a man named Euchenor, son of Polyidus the prophet, brave and wealthy, whose home was in Corinth. Euchenor had sailed for Troy knowing well that it would be his death. His good old father Polyidus had often told him that he must either stay at home and die of a terrible disease, or go with the Achaeans and perish at the hands of the Trojans. So he chose to avoid the heavy fine the Achaeans would have laid on him and, at the same time, to escape the pain and suffering of disease. Now Paris struck him on the jaw under the ear. The life went out of him, and the darkness of death enshrouded him.

So they fought, like a flaming fire. But Hector had not yet heard, and did not know, that the Argives were making havoc of his men on the left wing of the battle. There the Achaeans would soon have triumphed over them, so vigorously did Poseidon cheer them on and help them. Hector held on instead at the point where he had first forced his way through the gates and the wall, breaking through the serried ranks of Danaan warriors. Here the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus were drawn up by the seashore. Here the wall was lowest, and the fighting of men and horses raged most fiercely. The Boeotians, the Ionians with their long tunics, the Locrians, the men of Phthia, and the famous force of the Epeans could hardly hold Hector back as he rushed on toward the ships. They could not drive him away from them, for he was like a wall of fire. The chosen men of the Athenians were in the front, led by Menestheus son of Peteos. With him were Pheidas, Stichius and stalwart Bias. Meges son of Phyleus, Amphion and Dracius commanded the Epeans, and Medon and staunch Podarces led the men of Phthia. Of these, Medon was a bastard son of Oileus and brother of Ajax, but he lived in Phylace, away from his own country, because he had killed the brother of his stepmother Eriopis, the wife of Oileus. The other, Podarces, was the son of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus. These two stood in front of the Phthians and defended the ships along with the Boeotians.

Ajax son of Oileus never left the side of Ajax son of Telamon for a moment. Two dark oxen strain with all their might at the plow they are drawing in a fallow field, and sweat steams up from the roots of their horns, with nothing but the yoke between them as they break up the ground to the end of the field. In just that way the two Ajaxes stood shoulder to shoulder. Many brave comrades followed the son of Telamon, to take his shield from him when he was overcome with sweat and toil. The Locrians did not follow so close behind the son of Oileus, for they could not hold their own in hand-to-hand fighting. They had no bronze helmets with plumes of horse-hair, no shields and no ashen spears. They had come to Troy armed with bows and with slings of twisted wool, from which they showered missiles to break the ranks of the Trojans. So the others, in their heavy armor, bore the brunt of the fight against the Trojans and Hector, while the Locrians shot from behind them, under their cover. And so the Trojans began to lose heart, for the arrows threw them into confusion.

The Trojans would now have been driven in sorry plight from the ships and tents back to windy Ilium, if Polydamas had not spoken to Hector. “Hector, there is no persuading you to take advice. Because heaven has so richly endowed you with the arts of war, you think you must also excel others in counsel. But you cannot claim preeminence in everything. Heaven has made one man an excellent soldier. Another it has made a dancer, or a singer and player on the lyre. In yet another Zeus has planted a wise understanding, from which many men reap benefit and are saved, and he himself knows more about it than anyone. So I will say what I think is best. The fight has hemmed you in like a circle of fire. Even now that the Trojans are inside the wall, some of them stand aloof in full armor, while others fight scattered and outnumbered near the ships. Draw back, therefore, and call your chieftains around you, so that we can consider together whether to fall on the ships now, in the hope that heaven may grant us victory, or to retreat while we can still do so safely. I greatly fear that the Achaeans will pay us their debt of yesterday in full, for there is one at their ships who never tires of battle, and he will not hold aloof much longer.”

So spoke Polydamas, and his words pleased Hector well. He sprang from his chariot in full armor and said, “Polydamas, gather the chieftains here. I will go over there into the fight, and I will return at once when I have given them their orders.”

He then rushed onward, towering like a snowy mountain, and flew through the ranks of the Trojans and their allies with a loud cry. When they heard his voice, they all hurried to gather around Polydamas, the excellent son of Panthous. Hector kept going among the foremost, looking everywhere for Deiphobus, prince Helenus, Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus. He could no longer find them alive and unharmed. The last two were lying by the sterns of the Achaean ships, killed by the Argives, and the others had also been stricken and wounded by them. But on the left wing of the dread battle he found Paris, husband of lovely Helen, cheering his men and urging them on to fight. He went up to him and reproached him. “Paris,” he said, “evil-hearted Paris, fair to see but woman-mad and false of tongue, where are Deiphobus and King Helenus? Where are Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus? Where is Othryoneus too? Ilium is undone and will surely fall now!”

Paris answered, “Hector, why find fault when there is no one to blame? Of all days, this is the one on which I would least hold back from battle, for my mother bore me with nothing of the coward in me. From the moment you set our men fighting about the ships, we have been here, doing battle with the Danaans. The comrades you ask about are dead. Only Deiphobus and King Helenus have left the field, both of them wounded in the hand, but the son of Cronus kept them alive. Now lead on wherever you want us to go, and we will follow with right goodwill. You will not find us failing you, as far as our strength holds out. But no man can do more than is in him, however willing he may be.”

With these words he satisfied his brother, and the two went to the part of the battle where the fight was thickest, around Cebriones, brave Polydamas, Phalces, Orthaeus, godlike Polyphetes, Palmys, Ascanius, and Morys son of Hippotion. These had come from fertile Ascania the day before to relieve other troops. Then Zeus urged them on to fight. They surged forward like the blasts of a fierce wind that strikes the earth ahead of a thunderstorm. Such winds buffet the salt sea into an uproar, and many mighty waves come crashing in one after another on the shore, their arching heads crested with foam. In the same way rank behind rank of Trojans in gleaming armor followed their leaders. Hector son of Priam, peer of murderous Ares, led the way, with his round shield before him, a shield of ox-hides covered with plates of bronze, and his gleaming helmet on his temples. He kept stepping forward in every direction under cover of his shield, testing the ranks to see if they would give way before him, but he could not daunt the courage of the Achaeans. Ajax was the first to stride out and challenge him. “Sir,” he cried, “come near. Why do you think you can dismay the Argives to no purpose? We Achaeans are excellent soldiers, but the scourge of Zeus has fallen heavily on us. Your heart, of course, is set on destroying our ships, but we too have hands that can keep you at bay, and your own fair town will be taken and sacked by us sooner than that. The time is near when you will pray to Zeus and all the gods, as you flee, that your horses may be swifter than hawks as they raise the dust on the plain and carry you back to your city.”

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right hand, and the host of the Achaeans shouted, for they took heart at the omen. But Hector answered, “Ajax, braggart and false of tongue, I wish I were as sure of being son for evermore to aegis-bearing Zeus, with Queen Hera for my mother, and of being honored as Athena and Apollo are, as I am sure that this day brings destruction to the Achaeans. You will fall among them if you dare to face my spear. It will rend your fair body and make you glut our hounds and birds of prey with your fat and your flesh, as you fall by the ships of the Achaeans.”

Having said this, he went ahead, and the rest came after him with a cry that split the air, the whole host shouting at their backs. The Argives shouted back. They remembered their prowess and held firm against the charge of the Trojan chieftains. The noise from both armies rose up to heaven, to the brightness where Zeus is present.
